claims.text: Surface aluminizing will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The improvement from aluminizing will result from in situ formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale.
Untreated TiVNbTa is susceptible to oxygen ingress at high temperature.
TiVNbTa undergoes phase segregation during elevated-temperature aging.
Pack cementation or an equivalent deposition treatment can enrich the alloy surface with aluminum.
The aluminum-enriched surface will form a protective alumina scale during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed comparison is to be conducted in ambient air or pure oxygen at approximately 1000 degrees Celsius for 50–100 hours.
Aluminizing will produce a dense, adherent, and continuous alumina scale.
A continuous alumina scale will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the alloy matrix.
Limiting oxygen ingress will mitigate internal oxidation.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen interstitials promote phase segregation in TiVNbTa during thermal aging.
Depletion of solute interstitials from the TiVNbTa matrix during aging is associated with progressive softening.
Compared with untreated material, aluminized material will exhibit significantly lower oxidation-induced weight gain.
Compared with untreated material, aluminized material will exhibit less oxidation-associated microstructural degradation.
Compared with untreated material, aluminized material will retain greater hardness and tensile strength after exposure.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed to an oxygen-rich environment at 1000 degrees Celsius forms non-protective oxide scales and gains measurable weight.
Oxidation of the untreated alloy at 1000 degrees Celsius degrades its mechanical properties.
The intervention is anticipated to be effective near 1000 degrees Celsius under oxygen-rich conditions.
The durability of the alumina scale at substantially higher temperatures or under extreme thermal cycling is uncertain.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in weight gain and oxide-scale thickness, or failure to retain superior mechanical properties, would falsify the hypothesis.
